lead: Resolution is a single proof rule for clauses. A clause is a disjunction of literals. To prove a goal, you negate it, add that clause to the premises, and resolve until the empty clause □ appears. □ is false, so the clause set is unsatisfiable and the goal follows. Only a few universities teach this in the first logic unit, but SAT solvers, Prolog-style systems and program verifiers use it.
prereq: You need: CNF from 1.3, and predicates and quantifiers from 1.6.

sections.h3: Clauses, CNF and the resolution rule

blocks.text: A literal is an atom p or its negation ¬p. A clause is a disjunction of literals, such as p∨¬q∨r. CNF (conjunctive normal form) is a conjunction of clauses. Resolution uses two clauses that contain complementary literals p and ¬p. Delete both and take the union of what remains.

blocks.where: C and D are clauses, possibly empty; p is an atom; ⟹ here means 'resolves to': the right side is the resolvent of the two left clauses. The symbol ⊢ is kept for derivability, as in P ⊢ G.

blocks.text: If C and D are empty, the result is □. The rule is sound: if both parent clauses are true, the resolvent is true.

items: Convert every premise and the negated goal ¬G to CNF.
Write the clause set; remove duplicate literals and duplicate clauses.
Resolve two clauses with complementary literals.
Stop at □. If no new clause appears, no proof exists.

blocks.text: Resolution proves G from premises P when P plus ¬G gives □. This is proof by contradiction; see 1.7.

Predicate clauses contain terms. First rename bound variables so no two quantifiers use the same variable name; this is 'renaming apart'. Then remove quantifiers in this order: Skolemize ∃ while the quantifier prefix is still visible, then drop the remaining ∀ quantifiers. For ∃y: if no ∀ surrounds it, replace y by a Skolem constant a; if ∀x surrounds it, replace y by a Skolem function f(x) of every enclosing ∀ variable. For example, ∀x∃y Loves(x,y): ∃y sits under ∀x, so y becomes f(x), giving Loves(x,f(x)). Do not use one constant for y: the loved person may depend on x, and f(x) records that dependency. Only after Skolemization do you drop ∀x, leaving Loves(x,f(x)).

Resolution then needs unification: a substitution θ makes two atoms identical. Before unifying, rename the variables of one parent clause so the two clauses share no variable names; then unify. From {P(x), Q(x)} and {¬P(a)} use θ={x/a}; the resolvent is {Q(a)}. Apply θ to every remaining literal. In propositional logic, unification is trivial; in predicate logic it is the extra step.
Full unification algorithms and completeness proofs are left to advanced courses.

figure.caption: The tree resolves p∨q with ¬p to get q, then resolves q with the negated goal ¬q to reach □. The goal is negated before the proof starts.

spec.aria: A resolution tree ending in the empty clause: q is derived from p∨q and ¬p, then clashes with ¬q.

examples.question: Use resolution to prove q from the premises p∨q and ¬p. Show the clause form and every resolvent.
steps: The premises p∨q and ¬p are already clauses: {p,q} and {¬p}.
The goal is q. Negate it: ¬q. Add the clause {¬q}.
Resolve {p,q} with {¬p} on p. Remove p and ¬p. The resolvent is {q}.
Resolve {q} with {¬q} on q. Remove q and ¬q. No literals remain, so the resolvent is □.
□ means {p∨q, ¬p, ¬q} is unsatisfiable. Therefore p∨q and ¬p entail q.
examples.answer: The empty clause □ is derived, so q is proved from p∨q and ¬p.

traps: Do not resolve an implication directly. Convert p→q to ¬p∨q first, then resolve.
Resolution proves by refutation: negate the goal and add it as a clause. Forgetting ¬G gives no empty clause.
The resolvent keeps all remaining literals. Resolving {p,q} with {¬p,q} gives {q}, not □.
In predicate logic, unify before resolving. A wrong substitution such as {x/a} when atoms need {x/f(a)} gives an invalid resolvent.
□ is false, not a normal clause. It signals a contradiction, so the original clause set is unsatisfiable.

quiz.a: A clause is a disjunction of literals, for example p∨¬q∨r.

quiz.q: What does the empty clause □ mean in resolution?
quiz.a: □ is false. Deriving it shows the clause set is unsatisfiable.

quiz.q: Why must you negate the conclusion in a resolution proof?
quiz.a: Resolution is a refutation method. Deriving □ from the premises plus ¬G shows the premises entail G.

quiz.q: Resolve {p, ¬q, r} with {q, s} on q.
quiz.a: Remove ¬q and q. The remaining literals are p, r, s, so the resolvent is {p, r, s}.

quiz.q: Use resolution to prove q from p→q and p.
quiz.a: Convert p→q to ¬p∨q. Clauses: {¬p,q}, {p}, and negated goal {¬q}. Resolve {¬p,q} with {p} to get {q}. Resolve {q} with {¬q} to get □.

quiz.q: Why does resolving {p,q} with {¬p,q} give {q}, not □?
quiz.a: The complementary pair p and ¬p is removed. The literal q remains in both parents, so the resolvent is {q}. □ appears only when no literals remain.

quiz.q: In ∀x∃y Loves(x,y), why use a Skolem function f(x) instead of a single constant?
quiz.a: The witness y may depend on x. A single constant fixes one person for all x, which is stronger than the premise. f(x) keeps the dependency and preserves satisfiability.

beyond: Not for the exam. Resolution is the base of SAT solvers used in chip design and scheduling. Prolog runs a restricted resolution strategy. Modern provers add ordered resolution, paramodulation and SMT theories. Search for 'resolution theorem proving' and 'unification'.
